title: Laws of Motion — NIOS Official Summary
intro: This is the NIOS Senior Secondary Physics (312) Learner's Guide summary for Lesson 3: Laws of Motion. It covers the concepts of force and inertia, Newton's three laws of motion, momentum and impulse, conservation of momentum, equilibrium of concurrent forces, and friction (static and kinetic).

branches.label: Force and Inertia
details: Inertia: resistance to change in motion

branches.label: Newton's Laws
details: 1st: body at rest/uniform motion unless acted by force
2nd: F = ma (rate of change of momentum)

branches.label: Momentum & Impulse
details: Impulse = F · Δt = change in momentum
Impulse unit: N·s or kg m/s

sections.heading: Concepts of Force and Inertia
bullets: The property of an object by which it resists a change in its state of rest or of uniform motion in a straight line is called inertia.
Mass of a body is a measure of its inertia.
The change in velocity of an object can only be brought about if a net force acts on it.
Forces may change the shape and size of an object.
Forces also influence the motion of an object and can rotate a body about an axis.
Force is a vector quantity. For a body in motion, the velocity will change depending on the direction of the force acting on it.

sections.heading: First Law of Motion (Law of Inertia)
bullets: A body continues to be in a state of rest or of uniform motion in a straight line unless it is acted upon by a net external force.
This law identifies inertia as the property of matter that resists changes in motion.
It is valid in inertial frames of reference (frames that are not accelerating).

sections.heading: Momentum and Second Law of Motion
bullets: The product of mass m of a body and its velocity v is called its linear momentum p. Mathematically p = mv.
SI unit of momentum is kg m s⁻¹.
Momentum is a vector quantity.
Second law: the rate of change of momentum of a body is directly proportional to the net force acting on the body, and the change takes place in the direction of the net external force.
F = k Δp/Δt, and with constant mass: F = k m a. Taking k = 1 (with SI units) gives F = m a.
The SI unit of force is the newton (N) = 1 kg m s⁻².

sections.heading: Third Law of Motion
bullets: To every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction.
When two objects interact, the force exerted by one object on the other is equal in magnitude and opposite in direction to the force exerted by the latter on the former.
Mathematically: F₁₂ = −F₂₁.
Action-reaction forces act on DIFFERENT bodies, so they do not cancel each other in the free-body diagram of either single body.

sections.heading: Impulse and Conservation of Momentum
bullets: The effect of a force applied for a short duration is called impulse.
Impulse = F · Δt is equal to the change in linear momentum.
Impulse is a vector quantity with SI unit kg m s⁻¹ (or N·s).
Conservation of momentum: in an isolated system (no external force), the vector sum of the momenta of the bodies remains constant.
Applications: recoil of a gun (mv₁ + Mv₂ = 0 ⇒ v₂ = −(m/M) v₁), collisions, explosion of a bomb, rocket propulsion.

sections.heading: Friction
bullets: Force of friction is a contact force that always acts along the surfaces in a direction opposite to the motion of the body.
Static friction: f_s ∝ f_N, with f_s = μ_s f_N. μ_s is the coefficient of static friction.
Kinetic friction: f_k ∝ f_N, with f_k = μ_k f_N. μ_k is the coefficient of kinetic friction.
Values of μ_s and μ_k for a given pair of materials depend on the roughness of surfaces, their cleanliness, temperature, humidity, etc.
Methods of reducing friction: use of lubricants such as grease or oil between the surfaces in contact; flow of compressed and purified air between the surfaces in contact.

sections.heading: Equilibrium of Concurrent Forces
bullets: A number of forces acting simultaneously at a point are called concurrent forces.
If the vector sum of all concurrent forces on a body is zero, the body is in equilibrium.
An equivalent condition is that the body has zero acceleration — it is either at rest or moving with uniform velocity.

key_takeaways: Inertia is the resistance of a body to change in its state of motion; mass measures inertia.
Newton's First Law (inertia): a body continues at rest or in uniform straight-line motion unless acted upon by a net external force.
Newton's Second Law: F = ma (or more generally F = dp/dt). The SI unit of force is the newton.
Newton's Third Law: action and reaction are equal and opposite; the two forces act on different bodies.
Conservation of momentum follows from the second and third laws for an isolated system; it explains recoil, collisions and rocket propulsion.
Friction (static or kinetic) is a contact force opposite to motion; it can be reduced by lubricants or compressed air.

glossary.definition: The property of a body by which it resists changes in its state of rest or of uniform motion in a straight line. Mass is the measure of inertia.
A push or pull on a body; a vector quantity whose SI unit is the newton (N). Forces change the velocity or shape of bodies and can rotate them.
The product of mass and velocity: p = mv. A vector quantity with SI unit kg m s⁻¹.
A body continues to be at rest or in uniform motion in a straight line unless acted upon by a net external force. Also called the law of inertia.
The rate of change of momentum of a body is directly proportional to the net force applied, and the change is in the direction of the force. F = ma.
To every action there is an equal and opposite reaction: F₁₂ = −F₂₁. The two forces act on different bodies.
The product of force and the time interval for which it acts: J = F · Δt. It equals the change in linear momentum and has SI unit N·s.
In an isolated system (no net external force), the total linear momentum of the bodies remains constant.
A contact force between two surfaces that opposes the relative motion (or tendency of motion) between them. Static friction f_s = μ_s N; kinetic friction f_k = μ_k N.
